titulo.texto: Paquimé Effigy Vessels with Human Figures

frase_gancho.texto: Men and women of clay, seated and painted, who tell how life was imagined.

puente_narrativo.texto: We leave the Chihuahua desert and head down to the center of the country, to Guanajuato. Look for a clay vessel topped by a small human figure: it seems like just another container, but it hides a whistle.

guion_corto.texto: The potters of Paquimé made many vessels in the shape of a person. They are round-bodied pots with a human head peering over the rim and, sometimes, with modeled arms and legs. They are almost always seated, with the face and body covered in red and black lines on a light background. They belong to the polychrome pottery of Casas Grandes, among them the type called Ramos Polychrome. Specialists tell figures of men from figures of women by their anatomy and their posture. Several of the female figures show a swollen belly, and some seem to be pregnant. These vessels show the body and sexuality in a natural way, and are linked to fertility. They have been found in burials, and they are thought to have been used in rituals.

guion_largo.texto:
Notice how one of these vessels is made. Below there is a round pot, like the ones you have already seen. Above, a human face emerges from the rim, as if peering out from a hood, and for that reason some specialists call them “hooded vessels.” In the most complete ones, the potter also modeled arms and legs. In this way, the pot becomes a body.

The body is painted. The red and black lines on the light background seem to show tattoos, body paint and clothing, although scholars acknowledge that it is almost never clear which is which. The designs that repeat, such as step-fret patterns, triangles, spirals and zigzags, have been linked to rain and wind. They are the same motifs you saw on the [Paquimé pot](mna_s11_olla_paquime), now on a skin of clay.

Men and women were not represented in the same way. Those who have studied them tell one from the other by the features of the body and also by posture: the men tend to sit with their legs drawn up, and the women with their legs stretched out in front. In an analysis of some ninety figures, the men often appear smoking, something the authors link to the rituals of shamans. The women frequently hold bowls, perhaps to serve food at ceremonies.

These vessels do not hide the body. On the female figures there are breasts, wide hips and, at times, a swollen belly that looks like pregnancy. According to the same study, some women appear nursing or giving birth. On the male figures, the sexual features are also in plain view. For those who study them, fertility may have been as important in the rituals of Casas Grandes as the shamans were. It is a theme that already appeared in other halls, as in the [Pretty Ladies](mna_s03_mujeres_bonitas) of Tlatilco, made much earlier.

Who do they represent? There is no single answer. The magazine Arqueología Mexicana describes them as possible gods or high-ranking figures with access to the divine. Other scholars think that many of the male figures show mortal people, perhaps ancestors, and that some portray shamans in the middle of a ritual. It has also been proposed that men and women played different but complementary roles.

Many of these vessels have been found in burials. One of those kept by the museum, from Paquimé, was part of the offering in the burial of three children, according to the museum itself. It was made during the city’s period of greatest splendor, and it combines techniques from the southwestern United States with features that recall Mesoamerica. Others were used, it is thought, in rites to ask for fertility and rain.

These readings must be taken with care. Many vessels of this kind entered collections without a record of where they were found, and that limits what can be claimed. The interpretations are proposals, not certainties.

Before moving on, compare these figures with the [Paquimé effigy](mna_s11_efigie_paquime) you saw earlier. Same colors, same city, and yet each figure has its own expression. Together they form a collective portrait of people who lived about eight hundred years ago in a desert valley.

texto: Find the human head peering over the rim of the vessel
Compare how the figures are seated: with their legs drawn up or stretched out?
Follow the red and black lines on the body: do they look like tattoos, paint or clothing?

texto.Material: Polychrome ceramic (Ramos Polychrome type), with a light background and red and black paint
texto.Origin: Paquimé and the Casas Grandes region, Chihuahua

texto.pregunta: Myth: The human figures of Paquimé all represent gods or rulers.
texto.respuesta: Reality: There are men and women, with different features and postures. Specialists propose that some are mortals or ancestors, others shamans and others divine beings, and there is no single reading.
